translations.text: The life and way of life of our holy and honored father Apa Pisentius, the bishop and hermit of the mountain of Tsenti, recounted by John the priest on the day of his holy commemoration, which is the thirteenth of the month of Epip. In the peace of God. Amen.

The theme of this feast is full of joy on the day of our holy father, the Christ-bearer Apa Pisentius, who is full of light and gives off a sweet fragrance at all times—not only by day, but also by night.
All the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky rejoice, leaping and celebrating on the day of his honored festival, which came upon them, as the account will tell us as we go on.
I swore to remain silent and not speak of your achievements, because you have fled from human glory ever since you became a monk, before you became a bishop.
And truly, when we all gather together, one person has a prophecy, another has knowledge, another has discernment, and another has a revelation, so that all these things may serve to build us up.
But the holy apostle James declares in his general letter: “For someone who knows how to do good and does not do it, this is a sin.”
Let us understand whom the sacred apostle is speaking about when he says, “I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago—
whether he was in the body, I do not know, or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—was caught up to the third heaven.”
And I know this man—whether he was in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words,
which a human being is not permitted to speak.
Who, then, is the apostle speaking about, if not himself?
Since all the saints flee from the glory of this world, this was also the way of our honored father Apa Pisentius, whom God revealed to us in our own days,
as one who gives light to the whole world,
as salt that seasons everyone, according to what is written in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth.
But if the salt loses its flavor, with what will it be salted?”
And again: “You are the light of the world.”
He concealed his ways of life, but God revealed them in every generation to those who do his will and keep his commandments, as it is written:
“The Lord is near to everyone who calls upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of everyone who fears him, and he will hear their plea and save them.”
Do you therefore want to know that he hates empty glory and does not want anyone to go to destruction, or to learn about him through the way he conducts his life?
Listen, then, attentively.
One day, while he was still a monk, before God called him to become a bishop, he was living quietly by himself on the mountain of Tsenti.
His brother came to visit him, traveling with a faithful brother. They met the holy ascetic and received a blessing from his holy hands.
He asked them, “Do you have business in these parts?”
They answered, “First of all, we set out to come to you, visit you, and receive your blessing,
for our worldly concerns [?] even to visit you for many days now.
After that, we have a little business in this district that we want to settle. But pray for us, our father, so that God may travel with us.
If God gives us the opportunity, we will return to you again, greet you, and receive your blessing before returning to our home, if it is God’s will.”
The holy man answered, “Go with joy, but watch yourselves, my children. Do not sin.
For the world we are in is nothing, because it lasts only a short time.
Be careful, my children, in these villages.
Do not associate with an evil woman.
Do not take interest and become poor.”
If you have anyone in these districts, do not force him or harass him.
Instead, watch over the affairs of the soul, so that God will show you his mercy.
They answered, “Pray for us, our father.”
They left him and set out on the road, glorifying God for the words of instruction he had entrusted to them.
The holy hermit himself, Apa Pisentius, then stood up and began reciting from the beginning of the book of Jeremiah the prophet.
His brother went away with the faithful man who was traveling with him.
They carried out their task according to the word of the holy man, who had pleaded with the Lord on their behalf.
He made their journey go smoothly, and they quickly returned to him at the cell early in the morning.
When they came to him, they heard him reciting the words of holy Jeremiah with great calm and diligence.
They sat outside his dwelling for a little while, saying, “It is neither right nor fitting for us to call in to the holy man until he has finished meditating and praying.”
When he finished the prophet, completing the whole book, they got up to knock at the door. But he began the prophet Ezekiel.
They sat down again and did not call in to him.
Finally, he finished the entire prophet and fell silent, for evening had come.
When they knocked at the door, he answered them, “Bless me.”
He looked out at them in great amazement and spoke to them, saying, “How long has it been since you came here?”
They said, “We came early in the morning, but we did not dare call in to you until you had finished reciting.”
Immediately he wept and beat his chest. He said to them, “I have suffered a great loss today, and all the efforts I have made have been in vain.”
The holy man said these things because he was fleeing from the empty glory that people give.
He was grieved at heart because they had found out at all that he had been reciting.
So you understand, my beloved, that the saints desire the glory of God alone.
If not, listen to the holy hymn writer David saying, “I have longed for your commandments.”
“Look upon me and have mercy on me.”
The wise Paul, too, cries out to this day, saying, “For in this we groan, longing to clothe ourselves with our dwelling from heaven.”
And, “We have a building from God, an eternal house in the heavens, not made by human hands.”
Listen also to this great miracle that happened through him while he was still a monk, living quietly in the cell, before he became a bishop.
Once, on the third day of the feast of deliverance, he became ill in his spleen.
He did not tell any of the brothers that he was sick, for he had told them, “Pray for me
so that I may go to Father Abraham’s monastery and visit this brother who is there,
if the Lord allows me, and then return to you.”
He said this because he did not want anyone to know at all that he was sick.
But if someone inquires carefully, “Why did this holy man say this?”

let him read the book of blessed Job. He will find the Lord saying to him, “Do you think that I did these things to you so that you would be put to shame? Rather, it was so that you would be shown to be righteous.”
Paul likewise says, “I do all these things for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in it.”
When the holy Father Pisenthius had been sick for a week, the brothers had not looked for him, thinking that he was in the cave.
They said to one another, “Little Pisenthius has been away a long time. Let us look for him,
because perhaps he has become sick on the road, or perhaps exhaustion has afflicted him and he has been unable to get up.”
They sent a brother to his dwelling to look for him.
When he went, according to God’s providence, [?] saw the wonders of God.
Throughout all the days that he spent lying sick, the saints ministered to him, until the day when the brother went to him.
When the brother went to him, he found the door of the little room where he was open.
By an opportunity provided by God, when he pulled the door’s bolt, he called inside according to the brothers’ rule, “Bless me.”
For on that day it had so happened that the holy Father Elijah the Tishbite, of Mount Carmel, was beside him, visiting him. He had been sent by God to comfort him with his words.
When the brother had spent a long time standing and calling inside, “Bless me,”
the prophet rose to leave, but Father Pisenthius took hold of him, saying,
“I will not let you go until I have received a little more comfort.”
The brother, meanwhile, when he received no answer, went straight inside without thinking about it at all.
He found the two holy men sitting there.
Father Pisenthius was lying down, while Saint Elijah was sitting beside him, visiting him.
When the brother entered, he received a blessing from both of them.
He stood there, but he could not look into the face of the prophet Elijah because of the rays of light shining from his face like lightning,
as it is written: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
But the holy Apa Pisentius rebuked the brother.
He said to him, “Is this the brothers’ rule—that you should come inside without knocking?
If this were a ruler, would you be able to enter his presence without being announced to him?”
The brother answered, “Forgive me, my father. I have sinned. I waited at the door for a long time, calling out.
I thought that perhaps you were ill and could not get up. That is why I came inside to see how you were.”
The prophet answered, “This is God’s decree.
Certainly he deserves our greeting because of his good deeds. God has not despised him.”
When the prophet had said these things, he withdrew.
After he withdrew, the brother spoke to Apa Pisentius: “Where is this barefoot brother from, that such great grace
surrounds him like this? Truly, I have never seen anyone like this: he is joyful and filled with every kind of light.
And I tell you, my brother, the moment I took his hands and kissed them, great strength came into my body.
I was no longer weak; I truly became strong. I rejoiced like someone who has [?] at a watering place.
If I were to say that he belongs to this mountain, I have never seen anyone like him in our province, nor have I ever seen anyone barefoot like this man.”
He said to the brother, “Likewise, I will tell you. You must keep this matter secret and not disclose it.”
The brother answered, “Surely, then, even if necessity overtakes me after some time, I will not disclose it?
Why did you speak this way?
Do you not hear the angel Raphael speaking with the holy Tobit and saying,
‘It is good to conceal a king’s secret, but it is good to reveal God’s works’?
But I know that you hate the empty praise of people.
Tell me the whole truth about who this man is, and I will not trouble you.”
The thirteenth apostle, Apa Pisentius, answered the brother, saying, “When I left you, saying that I would go to visit the brother in Apa Abraham’s monastery,
I found that my body was weak.
I said, ‘Perhaps a fainting spell will overtake me on the road.’
My spleen made me ill from the moment I left you, and I saw no one until you came to me.
As my spleen continued to torment me severely, yesterday I begged the Lord to grant me healing.
When he saw my weakness and helplessness, he sent one of the saints to me and granted healing to my body.
And I tell you that this man through whom you received a blessing is Elijah the Tishbite, the man of Mount Carmel,
who was taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire and a whirlwind.
I beg you, my God-loving brother, do not reveal this mystery to anyone until the day of my death, so that you do not cause me grief.

When the brother heard these things, he felt great joy and comfort. He did not reveal the mystery to anyone until the day when the God-loving clergy of the Christ-loving city of Coptos took hold of the man who was truly worthy of the office of bishop, intending to bring him to the holy patriarch Apa Damian, the archbishop, so that he would ordain him as bishop.
You have understood, then, my beloved, that Christ loves whoever keeps the commandments of the monastic life and fulfills them without questioning,
and sends his saints to him. Not only that, but they see God, each according to his own vision, in the form in which he wishes to reveal himself to them.
If not, listen to the Scriptures inspired by God. They will open your eyes as they should, and in accordance with the statements we have made
about our lord and father, the bishop Apa Pisenthius, whom God revealed in our times as a protector not only of our district, but of the whole land of the Orthodox Christians.
Come into the first book, Genesis, and let us see how it speaks about seeing God.
As for Jacob the patriarch, when Rebekah heard the words of Esau, her older son, who was angry with Jacob because of the blessing Isaac had given him, she called Jacob and said to him:
“Look, your brother is angry with you because of the blessing with which Isaac, your father, blessed you.”
“Now get up and go to Mesopotamia in Syria, to my brother Laban, and stay with him until your brother’s furious anger turns away from you, lest I lose both of you together in a single day.”
Isaac also gave him instructions, and he went out. Jacob set off on the road. He said, “Go up to Mesopotamia.”
He came upon a place and lay down to sleep, for the sun had set on him.
He put a stone under his head and lay down to sleep. That night he had a dream.
He saw a ladder firmly set on the ground, with its top reaching up to heaven.
The angels of God were going up and coming down on it.
The Lord stood firmly above it. He appeared to him that night and spoke with him.
When he went up to Mesopotamia in Syria, God again spoke with him at night: “Lift your eyes and look with your own eyes at the white rams and male goats
mating with the sheep and goats, which give birth to multicolored offspring, colored with spots and speckles.”
God also said to him in a vision at night, “I am the God of Isaac. Do not be afraid.
Multiply, increase, fill the earth, and rule over it.”
When he had also blessed him with gold, silver, sheep, goats, and all the livestock,
he spoke with him again: “Return to your home, and I will be with you.”
Then Jacob returned with his two wives, Leah and Rachel, and their children and livestock.
When he reached the river to cross it, according to the words of holy Genesis written by the holy author Moses, he said, “A man encountered him and wrestled with him until dawn.”
When dawn came, Jacob said to him, “Tell me your name.”
He said to him, “Why do you ask about my name?”
“It is wonderful.”
And he said to him, “Let me go, for daylight has appeared.”
He said to him, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
And he said to him, “What is your name?”
He said to him, “My name is Jacob.”
He said to him, “You will not be called Jacob, but Israel will be your name, because you have prevailed with God and are powerful among men.”
He touched the joint of Jacob’s thigh, and his thigh was dislocated.
And he said, “I have seen God face to face.”
“My life has been saved.” And the sun rose over him when the image of God withdrew.
But we too, my beloved, ought to do so.
If God deigned to come down into the world and spoke with his creation to establish the salvation of their souls, how much more will he send his saints to comfort them in their sufferings?
Therefore, let no one disbelieve this statement that I have made about the holy Apa Pesentius, the bishop: that he was found worthy to see Elijah the Tishbite.
Otherwise, the written saying may be fulfilled in him: “God has closed the hearts of the unbelievers of this age so that they will not see the light of the gospel of Christ.”
And again: “Do not walk with unbelievers.” And again: “The unbeliever does not have a single obol.”
Our Lord himself, our God, our Lord and our Savior, cries out in the holy Gospels with his divine mouth concerning the man who brought his son to him,
who had an evil spirit with him, when he asked his father,
“Look, how long has this afflicted him?”
He said, “Since his childhood. And it often throws him into the water and into the fire to kill him.”
“But help us with whatever you can do, and have compassion on us.”
Jesus said to him, “All things are possible for the one who believes.”
The father of the little boy cried out, “I believe! Help my unbelief!”
He rebuked the evil spirit and immediately drove it out of him, in accordance with his father’s faith.
Again, through the power of faith, a woman approached him who had been bleeding for twelve years and whom no one had been able to heal.
She merely touched the hem of his garment, and immediately her bleeding stopped.
He spoke with her, saying, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

He also spoke with the disciples: “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from this place to that one,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”
And again: “You will say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.”
They also said about the holy Apa Pisentios himself that, when he was young and tending his father’s sheep, God opened his eyes, and he saw a pillar of fire before him.
There were other young children tending the sheep with him.
He said to the young children tending the sheep with him, “Have you seen the pillar of fire before us?”
They said to him, “We have not seen it.”
He cried out toward heaven, saying, “God, open the eyes of these young children so that they may see the pillar of fire, just as I too have seen it.”
And God listened to his voice. Their eyes were opened, and they saw it.
You see, then, my beloved, that when God chose Moses from his childhood, he spoke with him from a pillar of fire, from the bush.

As for Apa Pisentios, God came to him from his childhood, choosing him like Samuel, whom his mother gave to the Lord’s temple according to her vow. As David, the sacred psalmist, said: “Holy Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.”
They cried out to the Lord, and he listened to them. He spoke with them from a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the ordinances he gave them.
There was also a brother on the mountain of Tsenti who was very ill. His body had wasted away because his illness had lasted so long.
One day he longed for a little fish. He said to the holy Apa Pisentios, who was still a monk at that time and had not yet become a bishop, “I long for a little fish, but I have not found any.”
The holy Apa Pisentios answered, “God will certainly provide it for you today.”
“Cast your cares upon the Lord, and he will sustain you.” The prophet said, “He will never allow the righteous to be shaken.”
The holy Apa Pisentios himself took his pitcher to fill it with water, for it was the season of the rising, the rising of the water.
As the holy Apa Pisentios walked, he cried out to the Lord: “God, do not leave this brother’s heart sorrowful. Rather, if it is your will, grant him his request.”
“Do not leave him sorrowful, Lord.”
When he went out onto the embankment to draw water, there was a great abundance of water, for God had visited the land that year. Apa Pisentios looked.
He saw a large fish swimming in the water and wriggling.

Oh, this great wonder of God! Instead of the blessed Apa Pisentios going out into the water and pulling the fish to the bank, the floodwater and the water of the canals drew it along and brought it to that place.

He was still about to fill his pitcher with water, as he told us with his own mouth, bearing witness to us. So he took the fish and gave it to the brother, saying to him, “God has fulfilled your request.”
“The one who sent Daniel his meal does not hesitate.”
He said, “He is also the one who, by his will, prepared the fish for you today, because he did not leave you sorrowful over what you asked of him.”
Truly, the prophet spoke well when he said, “The Lord is near to everyone who calls upon him in truth.”
“And he will hear their plea and save them.”
The Lord will protect anyone who loves him.
When the children of Israel rose up against Moses and Aaron, they said to him, “What is this you have done to us?
You brought us up out of the land of Egypt,
where we sat beside the pots of meat and ate bread until we were full. Now give us bread and meat.
Otherwise, we will stone you.” And the whole assembly said that they should be stoned.
Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, “Lord, where will I find meat for these people to eat?
In a little while they will stone me.”
The Lord said to Moses, “I have heard your grumbling—the grumbling of the children of Israel that they directed against you.

Command the children of Israel, saying, ‘Prepare yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat. You will eat not for two days, nor for three, nor for ten days, but for a whole month, until it comes out of your nostrils.’”
And he brought quail from the sea, two cubits above the ground.
You have therefore understood, my beloved, that the prayer of a righteous person is very powerful and effective, as it is written.
As for Moses, the lawgiver of the old covenant, the moment he called upon the Lord on behalf of the multitude, the Lord acted according to his wish.
Likewise, the lawgiver of the new covenant, Apa Pisentios,

the moment he pleaded with the Lord on behalf of the brother who was a monk, the Lord did not cause him sorrow, but fulfilled his request, as it is written in the Psalms: “May the Lord fulfill all your requests.”
Listen also to this other great miracle that took place through the holy Apa Pisentios while he was a monk, before he became a bishop.
One day he went to the well from which the brothers drank water, to fill his pitcher with water.
When he went to the well, he forgot the rope and the bucket and did not take them with him.
When he stood beside the well, he prayed to the Lord according to the brothers’ custom and said, “Lord, you know that I do not have the strength to return to the monastery again to get the rope.
So command this water to come up to me, so that I can find a way to fill my pitcher with water and serve you for the rest of my days.
For you commanded your apostle Peter, ‘Walk upon the water.’”
When he finished the prayer, the water rose until it reached the mouth of the well, and he filled his pitcher with water.
Then he said to the water, “The Lord commands you: Go back down to your place.”

While the water was receding, a shepherd who was tending his flock of sheep among the thorn bushes approached the mouth of the well. He saw the water swirling round and round in the well until it went down to its place.
To whom shall I compare you, blessed Apa Pisentios?
Truly, you are like Moses the lawgiver, who made the sea divide to one side and the other, and the children of Israel walked through it as on dry ground,
while the water became a wall for them on either side, to their right and to their left.
He who spoke to the rock, and it poured out streams of water.

You too, O holy one, your prayer rose to the vault of heaven. The scripture was fulfilled which says, “He is the one who spoke, and they came into being; he is the one who commanded, and they were created.”
You became contemplative like the prophets and discerning like the apostles. You became a faithful steward.
For this reason, you were found worthy of the assembly of the saints.
God entrusted you with a multitude of souls.

You preached the good news like Paul, and you proclaimed it with your wisdom in the orthodox faith. You raised your voice in your discourses like a herald, calling out with your wisdom like a trumpet.
Who can honor you as you deserve, O holy and righteous one?
For you know hidden things before they happen.
You used to speak with laypeople in songs and parables, and you used to speak with monks through spiritual interpretations.
You used to speak with rulers in parables and mysteries.
You were not ashamed before anyone and did not refrain from telling them the truth [?], as it is written: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed.”
You used to guide those who came to you—to you, all of them [?]—to become believers.
And you gathered everyone to yourself in the bond of your love.
You obeyed Christ’s commandment. You built your house on the holy rock.
You bore fruit with perseverance and a holy and good heart.
You contemplated the spiritual meal. For this reason, you rested at the holy banquet.
You sought pasture and a good grazing place. For this reason, you also cared for the poor at all times.
You grasped the benefits of serving God. For this reason, you became a navigator on the sea of the holy mysteries, and holy like the three young men.
And a father to many poor people in our time, and a father to orphans in our days.
You used to proclaim peace to those far away, O God-loving father, Apa Pisenthius.
And you used to train those near you in sound teaching.
You became a spiritual merchant. For this reason, you generously gave your good things to everyone with great joy.
You sought and found, O God-loving father, Apa Pisenthius, the [?] of truth.
You knocked, and they opened for you. You asked, and God granted you all your requests.
A great benefit [?] in your time. Great stability came to the Christians.
The church flourished in your days and in your generation.
Your people rejoiced in your wisdom, and your children delighted in your holy mysteries.
The rulers longed for your words, and all the converts sought your mysteries.
You beheld the man whose name is the Sunrise.
For this reason, he filled you with the radiance of the Holy Spirit.
You completed the ark of the Holy Spirit to a cubit in length, like Noah.
You became a lamp shining throughout our whole district.
Righteousness and peace shone before you throughout all your days.
In your days, too, the foundation became radiant through your prayers and those of the saints who lived in it, namely Apa Colluthus and Apa Paham, these great saints.
And now, once again, by the grace of God, let us tell you another miracle that we heard from those whose entire hope rests in the truth.
A man from our district spoke with us about the holy Apa Pisenthius himself, saying, “One day I went and received a blessing from him.”
“When he came out from his presence, I met the holy Apa Paham. He said to me, ‘Did you receive a blessing from little Pisenthius?’”
“I said to him, ‘Yes, my father, but you are the holy one.’”
“He answered me, ‘Little Pisenthius truly is a holy man, and you received a great blessing if you met him. For it was at the beginning that he prayed and the cistern filled with water.’”
He said to us, “One day we saw a fire blazing in his house. We said to one another, ‘Why would little Pisenthius be lighting a fire at these hours?’”
They went up and looked at him through the wall. They saw him standing in prayer, with his hands stretched upward toward heaven. His ten fingers were like ten fiery lamps, shining very brightly.
But when God called him to this ordination to the priesthood, of which he was worthy, he went and hid himself because he understood its weight.
When the God-loving clergy sought him to seat him on the throne of the high priesthood, of which he was truly worthy, they searched for him and found him hiding in the region of Jeme.
When they seized him, he cried out, repeating the words of the great John, archbishop of Constantinople: “Oh, the quiet
“that I love! They will not leave me in it!”
Then they brought the holy man and seated him on the holy man [?]; they seated him on the bishop’s throne.
He did not pursue honor; rather, honor pursued him. Those who seized him testified to us, saying, “He acknowledged it to us with his own mouth.”
“Except that I must not disobey the one who sends me to this, even if you cut off my head or throw me into the sea, I will not obey you and abandon this quiet that God loves.”
“Or have you yourselves not heard what is written in the Psalms: ‘Be still and know that I am God’?”
They pondered among themselves, saying, “Who, then, is giving him orders? Is it a human being?”
They consulted with one another, saying, “Let us send word to the holy Apa Colluthus, a great man. He will reveal the matter to him and will not hide the affair from him.”

Then they went to the holy Apa Colluthus and said to him, “Our father, when we took our father Apa Pisenthius to ordain him as bishop, he did not want to undertake the ministry to which he had been appointed.”
“We have been pursuing him for many days, until we found him in the region of Jeme.”
But when he took hold of him, he wanted to decline his office.
Afterward he said openly, “I will not disobey the one who sent me. For even if you cut my head off, I will not obey you.”
“We therefore appeal to Your Holiness: meet with him one day and ask him privately, ‘Who sent you?’
For this matter is extraordinary.”
Then the holy Apa Colluthus asked him, “The God-loving clergy said, ‘Your Holiness said openly, “I will not disobey the one who sent me, for it is not my wish to hold an office of this kind.”’
Who, then, is it?” The holy Apa Pisentius answered, “Before the clergy came in to my humble self, I dozed for a little while. A voice came to me three times, saying, ‘Pisentius, Pisentius, Pisentius!
Look, the order of the church has come for you.
Do not decline the office to which you have been appointed by my chief apostle. Instead, get up and follow them.
Do not leave the church widowed.’
When I heard these things, the clergy called in to me.
I came out and followed them, placing all my concerns upon Jesus, because nothing will happen without God.”
You have therefore understood, my beloved, that these words of the wise Paul are true, when he says, “No one takes the honor for himself, but he is called by God,

just as Aaron was.” So too Christ did not glorify himself alone to become high priest, but it was the one who spoke to him, saying, “I have begotten you today,” and again, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”
And in this way he took his seat on the bishop’s throne in perfection, God having bestowed grace upon his face.
Like Joseph, no one could dare to look into his face without feeling fear, because of the fear of God that was with him.
For who can count the acts of mercy he performed for the poor—not only those of his own district? Rather, he would welcome those who came to him
and give them whatever they asked of him.
You also know that, before today, he made do with the small offering given to him to distribute alms in every city and village, as far south as Syene.

Whatever was brought to him each year according to the canons of the apostles, he would secretly send to God-fearing people in every city and village, so that they could give it to the poor during the winter, when the poor lack bread. He never forgot any poor person, as you know.

After some time, while our holy father Apa Pisentius was tending his flock with great care, he sent a letter to all the people of the district of Coptos, exhorting them: “Stop committing these great and grievous sins, as we have been informed,
lest God become angry with you and hand you over to the barbarians, who will afflict you.”
He also wrote in that same letter, “Unless you repent quickly, God will bring that nation against you without delay.
And even after you have been disciplined by that nation, he will not cease to stir up wrath against you through a nation
fierce and shameless in its appearance, whose people will show no respect for an old person or a child.
He will afflict you with sufferings like the plagues of Pharaoh in former times, until he throws all ten of them into the sea and his memory openly perishes.
Therefore let repentance remain constantly with you in your dwellings at all times. Let there be sighs in your hearts, and let fasting increase upon your lips at all times.”
For mercy triumphs over judgment, according to the words of James, the wise apostle.
For the third angel in God's greeting is the angel of mercy.
For compassion rescues a person from death and does not let him enter the darkness.
And it says, “It is better to show mercy than to store up gold.”
And: “With what you have, give to those in need.”
“Do not let your eye begrudge you when you give to those in need and act righteously.”
And again: “It is better to give a little in charity with righteousness than to give much with injustice.”
“And do not turn your face away from any poor person, and God will not turn his face away from you.”
And again: “Do not be afraid to give to those in need from the little you have,” as the holy man Tobit said.
Look at this rich man: [?] he neglected poor Lazarus. What did this do to him amid his punishments? He answered and said in anguish:
“My father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this fire.” And what he heard in return was a rebuke.
Abraham said to him, “My son, remember that you received your good things during your life, while Lazarus received bad things.
Now he is comforted here, while you are tormented. You did not show mercy; will mercy be shown to you? You had no compassion for the poor man.
You lived luxuriously on birds, [?], and other animals, eating the produce of your land alone, with insatiable appetite and inhumanity, drinking choice wine from bowls.
Meanwhile, you neglected the poor man and showed him no mercy from what you possessed.
And if he possessed even the smallest amount, you would unjustly deprive him of it.
If you will not give him anything from what belongs to you, at least spare him and protect his rights. Do not burden him with your oppression.
You know that you and the poor man were made from the same clay.
Do not cause him distress, lest God cause you distress.
There will be a place of judgment, and each person will be judged according to what he has done, whether good or evil.
These are the things that the God-loving father Apa Pesynthius repeatedly writes to all the people.
But how can I embellish the praise of the saint, except with words from his own mouth?
Rather, let us appeal to him to provide us with the material needed to deliver this praise, according to the measure of our lowliness.
We are not capable of reaching the height of his virtues. O good ascetic, adorned with the virtues of the Holy Spirit, with righteous deeds and all the commandments that are full of life!

Truly, even if I became entirely a tongue, I would not be able to honor you according to one ten-thousandth of your virtues. Even the little that we have managed to deposit in the treasury was prepared for us by your grace.

For we know that you have no need of our feeble tongue to speak a few words of praise to you, because your citizenship is in heaven, according to the words of Paul's sweet-smelling tongue: “But our citizenship is in heaven, the place from which we wait expectantly.”
Nevertheless, let us say a few things about the saint, to the glory of God.
Now, at the time when God brought the Persian nation against us because of our sins, Apa Pesynthius went to the mountain of Jeme and hid there because of the Persians.
For they had not yet taken the city of Coptos at that time; rather, it was their beginning.
I, Joseph, was traveling with him at that time, serving as his attendant.
I took some water containers and put them in the place where we were hiding, so that we would have them available for our needs throughout all the days we would spend in hiding.

Pay close attention to the account, so that you may marvel and give glory to God, who performs these great wonders through his holy ones, just as God did for the children of Israel in former times through Moses. He said to him, “Raise your staff and strike the rock, and it will pour out water for the people to drink.”
That is also how it happened here.

When he went again to his hiding place, I too was walking with him. We stayed in the place where we were hidden, and we spent many days there. All the little water we had left ran out. I said to my father, “We have no more water.”
My father answered, “God will not abandon us, my son. Rather, he will supply everything we need.
For he said, ‘Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself.’
And again, when Elijah the Tishbite was in the wilderness, the ravens brought him bread early every morning and again in the evening.
And when he slept beneath the tree called rathmen, he got up and found bread beside his head and a vessel of water.
The angels said to him, ‘Get up, eat bread, and drink water.’
Elijah ate the bread and drank the water, and he walked along that road for forty days and forty nights.
He ate no bread and drank no water.
So the one who supplied Elijah with spiritual food because he followed him with all his heart—
if he sees that our intention and our heart are directed toward him, he will take care of us too.
For he said through the holy psalmist David, “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you.”
For God knows what we need before we ask him, just as he said in the holy Gospel.”
After my father said these things to me, he walked away from me.
I threw myself onto the ground and pulled the cool sand over my chest as I lay stretched out, sleeping, burning terribly from the heat and thirst for water.
After my father had gone a very great distance away from me, he returned to me with his eyes full of light, like the lights of heaven.
He was completely refreshed, like someone who had bathed at a bathing place. He said to me, “John, I see that you are exhausted from thirst. Go, get water, and drink.”
I answered him, “My father, the water containers have been empty since the third hour yesterday, and there is no water at all in our dwelling places.”
My father would fast for three days at a time. Sometimes, too, when his body was free from illness, he would fast for the entire week.
Again he said to me, “John, why do you remain disobedient?
Go, get water, and drink, for I see that you are suffering terribly from thirst.”
He said to him again, “John, as I can see, you have become terribly parched from thirst, and you are suffering under the darkness of thirst for water.”
I answered him, “Yes, I have suffered. But this is the truth: when you went into the desert
and returned to me again, and I saw your face full of joy, shining with light like that of Moses the lawgiver, my physical condition
became stable, and I stopped being thirsty.”

He answered me, “If you have suffered like this for two days, then how much suffering falls upon those who are in the darkness of Hades, with the worm that never sleeps, the outer darkness, and the river of fire that flows before the true Judge, in which we will be tested!”
Truly, my son, it is a fearful and terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
After saying this, he said, “I think there is water in the containers. Have you forgotten [?]? Look, there is some in them.”
But I, this wretched John, am not worthy to recount that miracle which I saw with my own eyes, considering myself alone to be poor.
When I went to the place where the containers were, I declare to you, my beloved, by the fear that we will all face,
that I found them filled with water up to their mouths. Their water was white like milk and snow, and sweet like the waters of Gihon, which are turbid.
Then I went and asked my father, “I found the containers full of water. Where does it come from, my lord and father?”
He answered me, “Be silent, my son. The one who provides food for the ravens, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into a storehouse, is the one who has provided us with this water that we need.
For whoever casts his cares upon Jesus, Jesus will take care of him wherever he goes.”

So you have understood, my beloved, that wherever he goes, his entire hope is Jesus, as he remembers what is written in Jeremiah the prophet: “Cursed is the person whose hope rests upon a human being.”
Blessed is the person who has put his trust in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope.
He will be like a tree growing beside water, and his roots will not touch dry ground.
What shall I say, and what shall I leave out, among all the honorable virtues of this honored, righteous, and blessed man?
First I will speak about his devotion to God, and also about the grace that God gave him and the abundant gift that he bestowed on him, from his beginning to his end.
To whom shall I compare you, O blessed man, Apa Pisenthius?
I will compare you to Abel, who became the beginning of devotion to God and of the high priesthood of God, being the first to offer up his sacrifices and his offerings.
Therefore I will call your holy fatherhood blessed, because you became a father to orphans, and the widow’s mouth blessed you, O holy bishop Apa Pisenthius.
You became a father to the weak and a place of refuge for foreigners.
You became food for the hungry and water for the thirsty.
You became clothing for those who lay naked and a garment for those who lay naked.
You entered paradise in your mind. You ate from the tree of immortality.
You are wise in your silence; you are perceptive in your speech.
For your name has reached the ends of the inhabited world.
You became gifted in the wisdom of God and knowledgeable in the holy mystery.
You sought first his kingdom and his righteousness, and God bestowed all these things on you.
You entered the promised land in your mind. Therefore God gave you strength to overcome the hidden Canaanites.
You contemplated all the spiritual examples, and you understood all the parables of the Gospels. You paid attention to all their spiritual interpretations.
All the philosophers of the earth marveled at your wisdom, and they were baffled by your arguments in this age.
The scholars also marveled at your wisdom, and all the senators marveled at your mysteries.
For all who were suffering ran to you, and you helped them in your goodness.
You became a righteous man in our days and a model in our generation, O holy bishop Apa Pisentius, the blessed hermit.
The rulers became lovers of the poor in your days.
And they honored your devotion to God.
You were noble toward those close to you, and the Romans honored you.
You abolished the domain of the rulers [?].
And you shut the mouths of the wild beasts. The [?] were baffled, and the officials withdrew.
You defeated Amalek like Joshua son of Nun, and you defeat the Amorites like Israel.
You took up the full armor of God. Because of this, you were able to extinguish every flaming arrow of the evil one, and you fought against the devil’s schemes.
You grasped the shield of faith, and you shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace.
Your fame reached the ends of the inhabited world. You were wise before the rulers, like Saint Athanasius, and God gave you strength through the Scriptures.
You searched in your mind for the ages to come, and you pursued the hidden ranks—the wisdom of God.
You became a contemplative like holy Apa Pachomius, the father of the community.
God granted great stability in your days, and he graciously gave you his peace in your generation.
God brought forth your righteousness like the light, and he made your judgments like the noonday.
You kept God’s commandment. Because of this, your peace became like a river in full flow, and your righteousness like the vast deep.
Your abundant spirit will be like the morning star, and your offspring like the sand on the seashore, which has neither limit nor number.
And in your goodness you prayed for the whole world, and you urged everyone to return to God in repentance.
You taught the lawless the ways of God, and you turned the ungodly away from their ungodliness.
You raised up the sick through your holy prayers, and you pleaded with God for those possessed by demons.
To whom shall I compare you, O blessed father Apa Pisentius, the holy bishop?
You were faithful in our generation and righteous in our days.
You became a scribe in your senses and a shorthand writer in spiritual matters.
You became a chief physician, healing everyone with a good heart.
You grew tall like a palm tree in the righteousness of God, and you spread out in the wisdom of God like a plane tree.
You gave off a sweet fragrance through virtue, like cinnamon. The fragrance of your counsels reached the ends of the inhabited world.
You became a Pentapolis through Christ’s gift, and people recounted all your wonders in the cities of the whole world.
You became an interpreter of sacred mysteries like Moses, and a singer of sacred hymns like David.
For we have often heard your mysteries in your letters, and we have seen the stature of your holy writings in your letters, and your great wisdom.
You grew wings like an eagle, and you were transformed through the power of devotion to God, like a falcon.
God opened the eyes of your soul and showed you the gates of immortality, like the Samaritan woman.
And your mind stirred the meanings of Scripture like the plectrum of a lyre, and you sang hymns to him on a ten-stringed harp.
To whom shall I compare you, holy leader of the flock, Apa Pisenthius, the faithful priest?
Shall I compare you to Noah, whose holy sacrifices God smelled? For you tasted that work is good, and your lamp does not go out all night.
You made heavenly garments for yourself from fine linen and wool, and you planted a vineyard from the fruit of your hands.
You became righteous in devotion to God with all your heart and all your soul.
God gave you rain, as he did Elijah.
He made bitter things sweet through your ministry, as with Elisha.
The mountains became sweet in your days, and the hills brought forth flowers in your generation.
For you were building your children upon the immovable rock, Christ, and you were building an everlasting faith within them.
You became a source of rest for the Egyptians and of joy for foreigners.
You became one who labored in serving the poor, and a help to all who suffer.
You beheld the perfect spiritual lamb, and you rested among your children like Jacob.
[?] Afterward, you were laid beside your fathers, like David.
You became wise like Solomon, and you inherited the blessing from God.
Therefore you found the smooth paths. You finished the race, kept the faith, and received the crown of righteousness upon your head.
You established your offspring in Zion, Apa Pisenthius, and you gained a household for yourself in the heavenly Jerusalem.
You took up the sword of the Holy Spirit through every prayer and every supplication, because you overcame the world-rulers of darkness.
You beheld the sun of righteousness, who has healing beneath his wings. Therefore the eyes of your soul were enlightened.
You built the house of God like Solomon, and you completed its courtyard like Zerubbabel.
You walked in the [?] field. Therefore you found the treasure of the holy mystery.
You became [?] in your heart. Therefore God gave you the star of the light of his knowledge.
You have eaten the heavenly bread and rejoiced in the tree of immortality.
To whom, then, shall I compare you, O blessed man, great priest, Apa Pisentios?
I shall compare you to Jacob, whom God remembered in his sufferings because of his purity, and to whom he gave your inheritance.
I shall compare you to Joseph, to whom God gave the key to the kingdom.

I shall compare you to Samuel, who [?] the gifts of the high priesthood. I shall compare you to Samuel, who became a priest, to whom God gave the promise of the priesthood from his childhood, and also the gift of prophecy.
I shall compare you to the sons of Jonadab, who kept their father's commandment.
I shall compare you to the great apostle, Saint Peter, who stood in the rank of archbishop.
I shall also compare you to Paul, who cared for all the churches.
I shall compare you to Zechariah the high priest, whom God filled with the Holy Spirit.
For God gave you wisdom from his mouth, as he did to wise Solomon.
You contemplated creation like Moses. God abolished idol worship in your days, as in the days of Uzziah.
Who could come to you with a sorrowful heart and not return rejoicing?
O true comforter, according to the words of David the psalmist: "Your word has given me life; your word has comforted me."
Truly, you resemble Moses, whose face was glorified and who was exalted when God spoke with him.
You too, O lawgiver: the appearance of your face has been glorified through the power of God, who is with you.
He is the one whom all the saints befriended because of his purity and chastity, from the time when he was a monk, before he received the honor of being a bishop.
Who could ever look into your face without being afraid, O you whose eyes blaze like the morning star, continually casting out sparks?
O blessed is the womb that bore you!
If, then, I wish to recount all your accomplishments, I enlist scribes, like Moses the lawgiver and maker of laws, until I reveal your mighty deeds, O perfect saint, Apa Pisentios.
For you resemble the holy hermits Apa Palamon, Apa Pachomius, Apa Petronius, Apa Horsiesios, and Apa Theodore.
You resemble Saint Basil and Gregory the Theologian.
Who is as fit for the throne of the priesthood as you?

As for your wondrous mighty deeds, no one can comprehend them fully and recount them with ease. But what we have seen with our eyes and heard with our ears [?] an account of one of his mighty deeds—this is what we will recount now.

For you God-loving children know that when the days of the forty-day Paschal observance draw near, the holy archbishops of Alexandria send a proclamation south throughout Egypt, informing the bishops, the clergy, and all the orthodox people: "Prepare yourselves, for the days of the Paschal observance have drawn near." It also states on which day of which month you are to begin the holy forty days, and at what hour you are to end them.
Now the patriarch Apa Damian, the archbishop of Alexandria, sent God-loving clergy south with his holy proclamation, and they delivered it in each city.
Since Saint Apa Damian was the one who ordained Saint Apa Pisenthius as bishop of the city of Coptos,
when the God-loving clergy greeted our holy father Apa Pisenthius, they received a blessing from his holy hands and sat down.
It happened that day, according to God's arrangement, that some important men were sitting beside him.
A man belonging to our district, a shepherd who tended his sheep, came to him that day to receive a blessing from him.
At an opportune moment provided by God, the shepherd went inside after finding the door open. He bowed down at Apa Pisenthius's feet while the patriarch's clergy were beside him.
When he got up, he kissed his holy feet. He approached his holy hands to receive a blessing. He looked into his face and drew his hand back toward himself.
He did not give it to him, but cried out, “Who let this transgressor into this place, this bald-headed man?
Get out of here, you unclean man, you who are hateful to God!
Come and throw him out, John!”
I, John, his disciple, seized him and threw him out.
When I was a little way outside the door, I asked him, “What have you done today that the great man is angry with you

so intensely? Indeed, he spent the whole day cheerful and happy until you came in to see him. If you had not done something terribly wrong today, his anger would not have blazed against you so intensely,
even though the patriarch's men were sitting beside him.
Confess to me, for it is written, ‘Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be forgiven.’”
The shepherd answered, saying, “Why did I not die today when I woke from sleep?
While I was tending the flock today in this thorny scrubland, a woman I knew passed along the road.
In my foolishness, I seized her and had intercourse with her, thinking that the great man would not know.
The Lord is witness to my soul that, the moment he looked up, my conscience stirred within me all on its own, telling me that he knew what I had done.
A great trembling came over my whole body. I was about to fall flat on my face, but you seized me and brought me out through the door.
I very nearly fell flat on my face.”
That shepherd had brought some cheeses in a basket. He said to me, “Please take these few cheeses from me and distribute them to these people beside you. Since I have brought them, do not grieve me.”
I answered him, “We cannot accept them without the great man's instruction, lest he find out and become angry with me.”
He answered me, “I solemnly charge you by God Almighty to take them from me and give them to the poor on my behalf.”
When I heard God's awesome name, I was afraid and accepted them from him because of the oath by the Lord.
I took them and placed them on top of some other cheeses that had been brought to me that day.
I said in my heart, “I will not let the great man find out about me at all.”
That evening, when everything had grown quiet, he got up to give the [?] to the clergy.
He said to me, “If any cheeses were brought to you today, bring me some so that I can send them to the archbishop’s clergy.”
I took all the cheeses and put the shepherd’s cheeses on top of them.
When he looked at them, he said to me, “Bring me a platter here.”
He then told this riddle: “A man today has his eyes open, with no darkness coming from them, yet he covers his eyes day and night and walks like a blind man, although his eyes have light.
Will not everyone who sees him rebuke him, saying, ‘Why did God give light to your eyes, yet you preferred the condition of the blind, who walk in darkness all the time?’”
I tell you truly that when my father had finished saying these things to me,
he took all the cheeses that the shepherd had given me.
He separated them and laid them out on the platter. He said to me, “These cheeses, I tell you, belong to the shepherd whom I had driven out today.
When you drove him out, you took them from him.
Look, then, at whom you resemble.
You resemble Gehazi, who served under Elisha and called the man back, taking from him two talents and two garments.
Look, then, at how Elisha cursed him, causing Naaman’s leprosy to cling to his body.
Now get up and take them to him wherever you find him.
Indeed, even if midnight comes, you must not sleep in this place until you have given them to him.”
I said to him, “Forgive me, my father.
When I drove him out, he bound me with solemn oaths. I was afraid of the oath by the Lord, so I took them from him.”
He answered, saying, “Do not let the sinner’s oil anoint my head.

Paul, the voice of the good news, also says in his letter to the Corinthians, ‘I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.’ And again, ‘This [?], if he is sexually immoral, do not eat with him.’
And again, ‘God will judge sexually immoral people and adulterers.’
And again, ‘Let there not be anyone sexually immoral or defiled like Esau.’ And again, ‘Sexually immoral people will not inherit the kingdom of heaven.’
Go now and give them to him. Perhaps we will be able to save his soul from the devil’s grasp, for he too is a poor man.”
So I went and gave them to him that evening. I returned to my place according to the instructions of my holy father.
You have understood, then, that our truly righteous father Apa Pisenthius is a Spirit-bearer and a righteous man. If not, listen to the account and be amazed.
It happened again one day that my lord and father sent me on an errand concerning necessary matters in the district of Jeme.
It had grown very late before I returned, and night had fallen.
As I came along the inner road, two hyenas rushed at me while I was riding the donkey. They also rushed at the donkey, intending to tear it apart.
Indeed, their teeth almost reached my feet.
I cried out, saying, “Prayers of my father, help me escape the mouths of these wild beasts!”
Before the words had left my mouth, the wild beasts withdrew without harming me at all.
They acted as though they were being pursued, judging by the way they ran and their great haste,
when they heard the name of the great man, Apa Pisentius.
When I had walked a little farther,
some wolves rushed at me.
They threw a great deal of dust into the air, and a large cloud of dust rose over me.
As for the animal I was riding, I gave it up too.
I cried out again, “God, through the prayers of my holy father, Apa Pisentius, you are the one who rescued me from the mouths of the hyenas.
Rescue me again now from the mouths of these wolves!” Before the words had left my mouth, one of those wolves let out a loud cry.
They all withdrew through the prayers of my holy father, Apa Pisentius.
They all withdrew through the prayers of my holy father, Apa Pisenthius.
I went north to the mountain of Tsente, giving glory to God for what had happened to me, because he had rescued me from the mouths of the vicious wild beasts.
When I went north, I found the holy man studying the Minor Prophets.
I brought the animal into the stable.
My father looked down at me from the top of the tower.
He said to me, “John!” I answered him, “Bless me, my father.”
He said to me, “Did I not tell you that if it grows late, you should not come north until morning comes?
The wild beasts would nearly have devoured you, had it not been for God's mercy.”
You see, then, my beloved friends, that he knew about everything that happened. Wherever he was, he knew about what happened.
But he kept himself hidden through his way of life. He did not want to receive honor from people, just as the wise Paul said, “I do not seek glory from people, either from you or from others.”
If I wished to tell you all the deeds we witnessed through the blessed elder Apa Pisentius, the account would become very long.

But since Scripture writes to us, “It is good to make God's works known to everyone,” I will tell you a few things out of many about the virtues of this perfect man. After that, we will bring the account to an end.
Another day, a man came to him from the district of Coptos. His son accompanied him and had reached the age to be joined to the sacred marriage.
The two went in together. They bowed down and threw themselves at his feet.
The holy man said to the man, “Why have you not found a wife for your son?”
For that man was a native of Coptos.
The man answered, “He is a young boy, my father. He has not yet come of age, and he is sensible.”
The holy man answered, “Your son has indeed committed sexual immorality. If you let him, he will tell the truth.”
The man said, “If he has committed sexual immorality, here I place him in your hands, for you to do with him as you please.”
The holy prophet answered, “When you enter your village, you will meet a woman in the first street of your village.
She is the daughter of such-and-such a man. What is inside her will testify to you that it was your son who slept with her.
But do not think at all that I have said this on my own authority. No, I was informed through trustworthy people.
But if you listen to me, you will take her as a wife for him, since he has dishonored her.
Indeed, I will not allow him to join in worship until he marries her.
For the law commands that if a man sleeps with a young woman who has not been betrothed, taking her by force, he must marry her and live with her, giving her the bride-price appropriate for virgins.
And he must remain with the woman he has dishonored, whether she is poor or rich.
Now, then, the devil has caused your son to fall with this woman. Go and take her as a wife for him.
Do not let him sin, so that God calls you to account for the salvation of his soul.
For even if you join him to the sacred marriage and he falls into another sin, the blood of such a person will rest upon him alone.

Do not let him bring an accusation against you yourself before Christ’s judgment seat, saying, ‘My father did not find a wife for me,’ so that the entire responsibility for his sin falls upon you because you instructed him negligently, as the holy Scriptures indicate concerning Eli the priest: he instructed his sons negligently.”
The man answered, “I will observe everything you have told me.
For whoever disobeys you will be disobeying Christ, because the words that come from your mouth are words of life.”
The blessed man said, “May Christ be with you. Go in peace.”
He left him and did as he had instructed them, and their hearts were greatly relieved.
Another day, our holy father Apa Pisentius, the bishop, was traveling through the villages, visiting his churches.

When he had finished visiting them and was about to return to the monastery, he passed along the road by the [?], outside the canal. A farmer brought him a cow belonging to him, so that he would make the sign of the cross over her.
Look at the power of God!
The saint’s sign of the cross left a mark on her, as though his fingers had pierced into her.
When she gave birth, they found that the saint’s sign of the cross had left a mark on her.
And he sealed it on the outside, with a sign inside the small [?], in the shape of a white spear, like snow.
For everyone over whom the holy man stretches out his hand and makes the sign of the cross, whatever illness they have, is healed immediately.
Come, then, you whose hearts are directed toward God and the saint.
Beg him with tears and repentance, so that he may appeal to Christ to have mercy on us when we meet him. For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

If any of you dares to question the statement that I have dared to make—that the holy bishop Apa Pisentios is Christ’s friend—let him now come to the passage in the holy Gospel according to John and listen to God crying out through the mouth of his beloved saint, John the evangelist, saying, “You are my friends if you do what I command you.”
And again, “I have called you my friends because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father.”
And again, “You did not choose me, but I chose you.”
“And I appointed you so that your fruit might endure, living forever.”

You understand, then, my beloved, that whoever does God’s will is his friend and his brother, just as he said in the holy Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and my sister and my mother.”
One day they brought to them a little boy who was possessed by a demon.
He begged him, saying, “Please make the sign of the cross over him, for it is an evil demon.”
The saint asked his father, “How long has it been since this seized him?”
He said, “It has been seven years. I ask for your prayers, my father.”
“It throws him to the ground, and he thrashes about on it like a camel, and his eyes fill with mucus.”
“And many times we give up hope for him, thinking that it has killed him.”
“And he does not speak at all. Please help him, my father.”
Then my father called me, John.
He said to me, “Go to the basin in the church and bring me a little water so that I may sprinkle it on this little boy, for, from what I see, this demon is tormenting him severely.”
So I went into the church at the command of my lord and blessed father, the priest, and the person in charge of the place went into the sanctuary.
He filled the small container with water for me, and I brought it to the saint.
The saint made the sign of the cross over the water with his finger, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

He gave the water to the boy’s father, saying to him, “Take your son and go home. Give him some of this holy water to drink, which I have given you from the basin in the church. Believe in Christ, and he will heal him.”

My father did this so that he would not give him a drink himself with his own hands, and the demons come out immediately, and people boast about him, saying, “Apa Pisenthius has cast the demon out of so-and-so’s son.” For he did not want to receive praise from people.
When the man took his son to go home, according to what the man himself told me when he returned to us a few days later: “While I was still walking with my son,”

“when I had gone some distance away from you, the demon immediately threw him down onto the ground and made him thrash about. It cried out from within him, ‘Pisentios, are you going to drive me out of my dwelling place through the sign of the cross made by your finger?’”
Immediately the little boy was cleansed. I brought him into my house with joy, and it did not return to him until the day of his death.
After a few days, he went to the great man.
He bowed before him and took hold of his hand, saying, “I tell you, the little boy has been cleansed of the demon.”
His father testified, “I tell you, my father, that the moment I gave him a drink of the water that your fatherhood gave me,
the merciful Christ granted the healing of my son through your holy prayers.”
He answered, “Everything is possible for the one who believes. In particular, the water of the altar heals everyone who believes.

And do not think that this gift of healing is attributable to me. No, certainly not! Rather, it is the power of God present in his holy places for those who go to them with sincere faith and a heart without unbelief.
As for me, my son, I am the least in matters like these.”
When he had said these things, the man left him, glorifying God and thanking my blessed father.
Again, one day, a spirit of jealousy sprang upon a man’s heart.
He became jealous of his wife.
The devil, the hater of what is good, who envies and harms human nature, planted suspicion in her husband’s heart concerning a man, as though he had had intercourse with her.
But that woman was innocent of that matter, and the man too was innocent of the defilement alleged against him concerning the woman, as the account will tell us when we proceed.
The man threw his wife out because of the malice in his heart toward her.
His father and mother made every effort, but they could not persuade the man to live with her.
As the wise Solomon said, “Her husband’s heart is full of jealousy.” Not to prolong the account further, word reached the clergy of his village, and they barred him from receiving the holy mysteries.
The clergy informed my holy father about the matter.
My father sent for him, saying, “[?] trouble yourself so that I may meet you and give the necessary answer.”
The man shouted in the village as he went from place to place, [?], saying, “I will not go to Pisenthius!
What business does Pisenthius have with me?”
For that man was from Coptos.
While he continued shouting angrily,
for the sun had set that day,
God revealed what he had said to the prophet: “Leave judgment to me; I will repay,” says Christ.
A terrible illness came upon that man during the night.
He was tormented internally and was in agony. Crying out loudly, he said, “Take me to my father, Apa Pisenthius! I tell you, these things have overtaken me because of him.”
My father, please help me, for I have come to the agony of death. If you do not take me to him, I will find no rest.
His father and mother had given up on him, because he was going to die.
He said, “Let us do as he asks, even if he survives, since he said, ‘Take me to Apa Pisentios, the bishop.’ Surely, if we take him
to him, he will make the sign of the cross over him, and he will stop suffering.”
For this was at the beginning of my father’s time as bishop.
They brought him up to the mountain to my father. They called out, and I went outside to them.
His father said to me, “John, if you have ever seen me before, please notify the great man.
For my son is in danger of dying, and I trust in God that, if he makes the sign of the cross over my son, he will find relief at once.
He asked me, ‘Take me to Apa Pisentios, and I will stop suffering, for I am being tormented on his account,
if I said something to him in my foolishness, not knowing what I was doing.’”
His son also cried out to me, “John, please bring my plea before the great man, for the agony of death has overtaken me.
Look, you can see me in my distress.
Why did my mouth not close, and why did I not die before I spoke that day?
Go quickly and tell my Christ-like father, Apa Pisentios, about my suffering.
Help me, and do not leave me to die at your door.”
When I heard these things from the man and his son, I went inside and told my father about the man and his son.
He said to me, “Leave him alone until he has been properly punished, for he is undisciplined.”
I answered him, “If we leave him a little longer, he will die.
Only a little breath remains in him. And earlier, when I saw him, he had already been punished.”
My father said to me, “Let him come in.”
When he came in with his father, he threw himself down at my father’s feet for a long time.
My father said to him, “Get up, you undisciplined man.”
The man answered, “As Christ lives, even if I spend another three days lying at your feet, I will not get up unless you place your feet on my head.”
My father grasped the hair of his head.
He raised him up and said to him, “Get up. Look, Christ has granted you healing, if you will listen to me again.”
The man replied, “The distress from which your prayers saved me was [?]. Even if I have another two years to live, I will never dare to disobey you.”
My father answered him, “These things happened to you because you sent your wife away without cause.
As for what you suspected her of doing with the man, they are both innocent.
But I tell you, if you want to be fully convinced in your heart about her and the man whom you suspected of wrongdoing because of her—
for, my son, people look only at outward appearances, but God looks at the heart—
when you go into your house, bring your wife into the house.
God will give you an opportunity with her.
And I think she is pregnant, and she will bear you a son. The accusation made against her is not true.
But believe me: she is innocent.
If she bears a daughter, however, do not stay with her, but send her away.
She was not innocent of the charge brought against her, but violated her marriage.
But if the child she bears is male, the accusation brought against her is not true.
Rather, she is innocent of what they suspected her of.
But if you want to put her under oath, I do not forbid you, for God's law commanded this:

‘If a man's wife transgresses, and he neglects her through forgetfulness, and someone sleeps with her, having sexual intercourse with her, and she conceals it from her husband so that he does not know about her, and she has not conceived, and no witnesses stand against her, they shall bring her before the priest. He shall put her under oath and give her the water of the curse to drink.’
If the accusation made against her is true, that water causes her body to waste away.
But if she has been slandered, she conceives a son.
Now then, my son, if you are convinced—otherwise, put her under oath. I do not forbid you.”
The man answered, saying, “From the moment your fatherhood spoke with me, my heart became fully convinced. And I will never again stop obeying you.”
He received a blessing and left him.
He went to his house with his father, glorifying God and the holy Apa Pisentius.
When he entered his house, he was reconciled with his wife and fathered a son, according to the word of the apostolic Apa Pisentius.
The man named his son Pisentius.
He stayed with her from that day until the day of his death.

The holy man performed three interconnected miracles: the woman whom he saved from the false accusation made against her; the man whom he set free; and her husband's heart, which he purified of the schemes of the one whose power is over the [?] within him, namely Satan.
He made the married couple reconcile with each other once again.
Truly, your wonderful life is exceedingly great, O angel of the Lord of hosts!
For who could recount all the wonders that happened through you in your childhood, together with those that happened during your life as a monk?
As for those that happened through your hands after you became a bishop—those concerning which you give orders and do not want anyone to know—no one can reach the end of them.

But do not let the soul of that blessed man find fault with me because I have spoken these few words of praise about him. And I think we have gone beyond the proper measure in speaking these few, very insignificant words.

But let us obey the apostle’s instruction, by which he commands us, saying, “Give everyone what you owe them: tribute to whom tribute is owed, tax to whom tax is owed, fear to whom fear is owed, and honor to whom honor is owed.”
Truly, you deserve every honor and all glory, just as the psalmist David said: “Bring honor and esteem to Christ; bring glory to his holy name.”
Listen also to this other great wonder, and give glory to Christ.
It happened again that a man came to him and pleaded with him, saying, “Please be kind and help me, my [?] father, for I owe a man [?] gold coins, and they are pressing me for them.
I have not been able to find them to give to him.
And I have nothing there except one son, my only child. They have taken him into custody
and put him in prison, wanting to make him a slave.
I appeal to you as a father to have compassion on me,
if you can give me a little so that I may go and pay it, and they may release my only son to me.”
Now that man was a soldier from a foreign country, living in the parts of the mountain of Teilaj.
When he heard of my father’s reputation, that he was a bishop who gave charitable gifts, he got up
and came to him with his wife, wanting to test whether he was charitable or not.
He had put the woman aboard the boat and made her stand there. He had exacted thirty-nine gold coins from her aboard the boat.
Perhaps he had shed a man’s blood and taken them.
He came to my father, wanting to test him to see whether the things he had heard about him were true or not.
On the day when he came to the holy bishop Apa Pisentius, he found him inside the holy assembly of Tsenti, conducting the general service.
For it was the feast day of the archbishop and patriarch Apa Severus, archbishop of Antioch.
He sat down to wait until he came out of the assembly, so that he could bow before him and tell him the matter that I have already related.
When the great men heard this, he said to the soldier through the interpreter, “Pisentius’s place is not a place for mockery.
Go and take the thirty-six gold coins from your wife, who is aboard the boat at the riverbank.
As for the money, look: it is tied up in a cloth in her possession—the money you brought to test us with.
See what you will do with them, since you shed a man’s blood
and took them from him, saying, ‘I brought them to give as charity for the salvation of my soul.’”

Truly I tell you, even if they give the whole world in charity on your behalf, you will find no mercy unless your blood is shed, just as you shed your neighbor’s blood. As it is written, “Whoever sheds a person’s blood, his own blood will be shed in return, because humanity was made in the image of God.”

When the man heard these things, he was utterly astonished. He had thought that the matter would be hidden from the new Elisha, not realizing that the same Spirit speaks through the prophets and the apostles.
For this God hears these things.
He left him weeping and went home deeply distressed. You now understand that I did not lie at the beginning of this eulogy when I said that the blessed Apa Pisentios, too, was a bearer of the Spirit.
For whenever anyone went to him, he knew what business had brought them to him as soon as he looked into their face.
But he hated the empty praise of people and hid his way of life from us, so that no one could discover its full extent.
It also happened at the time when he was fleeing from the Persians and living quietly in the mountain of Jeme.
He went a little way away from us to pray.
After he had spent three or four hours walking and praying from place to place,
and no one could determine the full extent of the prayers he offered by day and by night.
He would pray four hundred times during the night.
He turned toward me and spoke to me, Joseph.
He said to me, “Be on your guard, because I came across a large dragon on the mountain today.
It is not far from us, but I trust in God that he will not leave it near us.”
Early, when dawn broke, I looked into the distance, about a bowshot away.
I saw many birds and vultures settled on a rocky cliff.
He called me and said to me, “I think God has struck down the dragon.”

He spoke again and said, “Why do you not pay attention to the sayings of the Scriptures and understand them, as the wise David said: ‘You have made the Most High your refuge. No evil will be able to approach you,

nor will any plague be able to approach your dwellings. You will step upon a snake and an adder, and you will trample a lion and a dragon. Because he has trusted in me, I will save him. I will shelter him because he has known my name.
He will cry out to me, and I will hear him.’”
When God wished to transfer him to the dwelling of those who rejoice, the place from which pain, sorrow, and sighing have fled, the dwelling of the prophets, the patriarchs, and the apostles—
for he is a patriarch like Abraham, and he is an apostle like the apostles; he is an apostle and a prophet among the prophets, like Samuel and the one after him.
He is a faithful high priest like Moses and Aaron and those after them.

When he entered his final illness, in which he would find rest, it was the month of Epip in the fifth year. He called me during the night of the eighth of Epip and said to him, “Joseph, is anyone with you?”
I said, “There is no one except Moses and Elisha, the priests, who have come to visit you.”
My father called out, “Moses, Moses, Moses!”
“Put your life in good order.
You know how you have behaved in my presence.
Take good care of my papers, because you will need them, and your [?], that is, the [?] there.”

He turned again to Elisha the priest and said to him, “Elisha, take good care of the brothers, and hold firmly to the things I have entrusted to you. Ring the bell at the proper times, so that the brothers will say their prayers according to the cycles of the seasons and their souls will benefit through you.”
Elisha answered, “My father, I am close to going to join all my fathers.
If you are going to die, it is better for me to die first. For if the pillar on which I am supported falls, the devastation of the mountain of [?] has drawn near.
Where will we find someone else to shepherd us as you do, O my lord and holy father, if you too depart?
You have finished steering your ship toward a good pasture.
You have prepared yourself and will not be shaken, according to the words of the joyful man David: ‘I prepared myself and was not shaken.’
For we will be deprived of you and become orphans from this day onward.”
My father answered, “Indeed, five more days have been granted to me, beginning at the third hour today.”
I answered him, saying, “What has happened to you that you have said these things?”
He said to me, “Before I spoke with you, a trance came over me. A man of light came and stood before me.”
He said to me, “Pisentios, Pisentios, Pisentios,” three times.
Prepare yourself, for you have five more days in this world, and then you will come to me.
When he had said these things to me, he withdrew at once.
“Look, I am going to join all my fathers.”

When my father said these things to us, a great cry of weeping immediately arose among us, because we were going to be deprived of such a good father, one who comforted those in sorrow and offered repentance.

I declare to you before the Lord that, when my father heard about the Persians, he kept none of the poor’s possessions for himself. Even the [?] beside his head—he had it taken apart and gave it as alms to the poor.

The things he gave with his own hands, those he instructed me to give and I gave, and those he sent through trustworthy people from village to village, distributing them according to each person’s need—no one can know their full amount,
except God alone, who will give him glory for them all.
I said to my holy, Christ-bearing father, Apa Pisentios, “Perhaps, my father, you think we will not return, since this time you have left no possessions stored away for us?”
