My father answered, “We will return by God’s will, my son. And everything we have given to the poor,
Christ will give it all back to us doubled.”
What shall I say, or what shall I recount of the mighty deeds of this righteous man?
But let us return to his laying his body down.
For he had spent three days without eating or drinking or speaking with us or turning from one side to the other. Instead, he lay like the dead in the place of the great cell.
On the night of the twelfth of the month of Epip, they called, “John!” I answered, “Bless me.”
He said to me, “I have come near the end, and I will finish my course at sunset tomorrow, which is the thirteenth.
But take care: do not let anyone carry my body away from the place that I had them dig for me.
During these three days that I have spent, I have not spoken with you, while standing before God. And they have taken my account since the ninth hour yesterday.
I say that God will have mercy on me.”
I said to him, “Please, my father, take a little food, for you have tasted nothing for four days.”
My father answered me, “My son, am I to eat anything else after the judgment?
I say that I will not taste any food belonging to this world
until I go to Christ and break my fast in his presence.

When dawn broke on the thirteenth of Epip, he said to me, while other important men were sitting beside him, “John, you know that I have completed everything, for I have left nothing belonging to the bishopric of the city of Coptos still attached to me.”
I have only one full-weight gold coin, which I have had since the day I was tonsured in my cell as a monk.
I earned it through the work of my hands and have kept it until today, so that I may cover my body with the work of my own hands and not place a burden on those who come after me,
and have them say, ‘You have gone beyond what is proper.’

But you, Joseph, use it to buy a shroud for my body. Do not put anything else on me except the tunic they clothed me in, my monastic habit, my hood, my belt, and my cloak. Prepare my body and bury me.
And I think: look, the field has been laid waste.
Look, the place is full of jackals, because the fence has been torn down. Each person will do as he wishes.
Whatever each person does, no one will rebuke him, because the fences have been torn down.”
When our holy father Apa Pisenthius, the holy bishop, had said these things, he suddenly fell silent and did not speak with any of us.
He opened his mouth and gave his spirit into God's hands at sunset on the thirteenth of Epip, in the fifth year.
We lifted his holy body and brought it into the holy sanctuary of the community of Tsenti.
We prepared his body according to the instructions he had given us.
We spent the whole night reading around him.
Afterward, we celebrated the Eucharistic offering over him.
We took him to the mountain where he had made us dig while he stood among us.
We buried him on the fourteenth of that same month, Epip, in the peace of God. Amen. 99.
Written in Thoth, in the fourth indiction, in year 722 reckoned from the holy martyrs, year [?].

I, Victor, the least of deacons, son of the blessed Mercurius, deacon, son of the blessed Eponychus, archdeacon of Saint Mercurius the great commander, from the city of Latopolis, wrote this book. Everyone who reads the book, pray for me, so that the Lord may bring my pitiable life to a pleasing end. Amen.

[?] Through the diligence and care of our God-loving brothers, who do not love charity: Michael, the archdeacon and monk, and our brother Zechariah, the second deacon and monk of Saint Mercurius the commander, on the mountain of Tbo.

They prepared this book and placed it in their monastery so that it might be read for the benefit and full assurance of those who listen attentively. May the Lord Jesus Christ grant them a long life and endurance, and save them from the snares of the devil and from wicked people.

May he place blessing, abundance, and salvation in their monastery. May he preserve the life of our father, the superior, Abba Abraham, and the whole assembly of the cross-bearing brothers who live in their monastery, each one by name. May he bring their holy blessings down upon my lowliness. For when they leave the body, may they receive an inheritance with the fathers of the community: Apa Pachomius, Apa Theodore, Apa Palamon, Apa Petronius, Apa Horsiesius, and all the fathers of the community. Amen. May it be so for all of us. Amen.
